column3: Near-verbatim parallel joins the dead, deafness, call, and turning away.
Battlefield turning of backs supplies only a distant physical image of withdrawal.
Uses the same turning-away image but not blocked reception of a call.
Directly states that the deaf do not hear the call when warned.
The adjacent eschatological sign does not clarify deafness or refusal to hear.
Retreat in battle offers a secondary image of turning backs, not receptive refusal.
Directly asks whether the deaf can be made to hear despite lack of understanding.
The local praise and challenge about association add no hearing or turning relation.
Hearing granted without inward good still ends in turning away, closely explaining the limit.
Directly pairs making the deaf hear with guiding those in manifest error.
Turning away from the messenger and dismissing him sharpens active rejection of the call.
Resurrection of the dead is relevant only to the literal death image.
Hearing a faint sound on the Last Day does not explain present refusal of warning.
Immediate continuation: only believers can be made to hear, while the blind remain in error.
Describes the closure of hearing and sight that follows rejection.
Absence of vain speech in Paradise is unrelated to inability to hear a call.

Defines the deaf and mute who do not reason as the worst responsive failure.

The summons to submit supplies limited local context for response to authority.
Misplaced allegiance uses turning language but not hearing or warning.
God hearing prayer is a different direction of hearing from the focus.

God as hearer of prayer does not clarify human deafness to warning.

Not turning backs is a covenantal battlefield obligation, not a reception image.

The prayer about divine promise does not illuminate refusal of a call.
Striking faces and backs at death uses bodily direction without receptive refusal.
Revival after death adds a general literal counterpart already covered more directly.
Noah's warning about corrupt descendants does not add to the focus's mechanism.
Reward and safety for good deeds are only broad nearby judgment context.
The question about dying concerns enduring bliss, not deafness or turning away.

The missing hoopoe scene has no usable relation to reception of warning.
Universal mortality gives only a literal background for the dead image.
Reviving dead earth supports the literal possibility behind death imagery, without the reception axis.
Calling the messenger mad despite truth expresses rejection of a delivered message.
The retreat of stars is a temporal marker, not turning from a call.
Hypocritical verbal testimony supplies a distant contrast to genuine inward reception.
Guidance and mercy for believers broadly echo the responsive group in the focus.
Near-verbatim counterpart: the living and dead differ, and those in graves cannot be made to hear.
Listening attentively to the Quran and returning as warners provides a productive inverse response.
Resurrection skepticism supplies local death context but no hearing relation.
Turning from remembrance identifies attention deliberately withdrawn from divine reminder.
Reviving dead land supports resurrection imagery only.
Near-verbatim parallel: the blind in error cannot be guided and only believers hear.
Rejoicing while turning away is a remote image of hostile withdrawal.
Even speech to the dead cannot compel universal guidance, directly testing the focus's boundary.
The local consequence of failing to be certain about signs develops persistent nonresponse.
Turning away together with arrogance names a compact posture of rejecting the warning.
Competing qiblahs and refusal to follow signs concern a different directional dispute.
The hoopoe's certain report does not clarify hearing or rejection.
The bare mention of one who turns away adds little after clearer refusal passages.
Instruction about lowering one's voice is not about hearing a divine call.
Flight from death extends bodily retreat but not the focus's receptive failure.
The night turning away is a cosmic time image without a response relation.
Human persistence in asking for good is not inability to hear warning.
The trumpet-day scene is broad local judgment context only.
The life-death-return sequence supplies a general literal backdrop already covered.
Direct simile of a call heard only as sound, followed by deafness and lack of understanding.
The call to Moses is not a parallel for refusal to receive a warning.
Punishment follows the combined acts of denial and turning away.
Only those who hear respond; the dead are raised by God, directly paralleling both clauses.
The messenger has delivered his charge even if the audience turns away, clarifying prophetic limits.
Denial and turning away form the active refusal whose outcome is stated in the passage.
Questions whether invoked objects can hear their callers, a useful contrast in hearing and calling.
Divine judgment is general local context after more direct response passages.
Frantic flight toward refuge is only a physical retreat parallel.
Moses flees in fear, a distinct and non-rejecting use of turning away.
The queen's throne and rule do not clarify the focus's reception theme.
The command to turn away precedes an unavoidable caller, usefully contrasting present refusal and final summons.
The ban on battlefield retreat is a distinct legal-military use of turning backs.
Gathering deniers is broad local judgment context but adds no response mechanism.
Correcting a judgment of death is only a remote literal counterpoint.
The prohibition of arrogant walking does not address hearing or turning from warning.
Lot's people expel the righteous; the scene adds no hearing or call relation.
The faithful are not deaf and blind when reminded of signs, a clear positive countermodel.
The messenger's status supplies only general authority for the call.
Deniers are challenged for rejecting signs without encompassing them in knowledge, extending local nonresponse.
Turning away after covenant is a broad antecedent of refusal but now redundant.
Intercession and ransom on judgment day do not clarify blocked hearing.
Being brought from death to life and given light gives a strong inverse of dead, unresponsive darkness.
Pharaoh's promise of proximity to magicians has no focal connection.
Turning away from a divine call leads to replacement, extending the consequence of refusal.
Life and death devoted to God provide only a broad theological contrast.
Uncompleted death in punishment is a different use of death imagery.
The distribution command and obedience rule do not clarify deafness to warning.
Jacob's grief-driven turning away is not rejection of a call.
On the Day, reports become obscured; this is only a remote consequence of denial.
Unknown time and place of death do not explain the focus's dead-hearing metaphor.
Sealing hearing, hearts, and sight gives a direct mechanism for the focus's inability to make people hear.
The deaf, mute, and blind who do not return form a concise parallel to unresponsive turning away.
Hearing a caller to faith and responding supplies a clear positive inverse of the focus.
The claimed hearing paired with disobedience directly exposes a refusal that is not mere lack of sound.
The sealing of hearts after rejection helps explain the focus's image of disabled reception.
Assuming no trial leads to blindness and deafness, directly linking denial to impaired perception.
Covers on hearts and deafness in ears explain why signs and recitation fail to produce belief.
Deniers as deaf and mute in darkness closely parallels the focus's incapacitated hearers.
Given insights make sight a responsible response, providing a useful inverse to inner blindness.
Hearts and eyes are turned away after initial disbelief, extending the focus's account of persistent refusal.
Hearts, eyes, and ears left unused define a comprehensive failure to understand and hear signs.
Calling to guidance without any following is a direct parallel to the ineffectual call in the focus.
Whether called or left silent, they do not follow guidance, sharply stating the limit of exhortation.
It warns against claiming to hear while not truly hearing, directly distinguishing sound from reception.
Responding to the divine call is explicitly described as coming to life, the positive counterpart to the dead.
Sealed hearts and consequent lack of understanding provide a related account of nonresponse.
Hearing, sight, and hearts are given capacities, contrasting their closure in the focus.
A hidden veil before those who reject the afterlife explains why Quranic recitation is not received.

Reminders are met by turning away, covered hearts, and deaf ears; it also states that calling cannot guide them.
Turning from remembrance culminates in resurrection blind, directly joining refusal, turning, and impaired perception.
It relocates blindness to hearts rather than eyes, clarifying the figurative force of the focus.
Verses recited to them are answered by turning back on their heels, a close refusal-of-recitation scene.
It questions whether most of them truly hear or understand, directly matching the focus's hearing-and-reason axis.
Warning and non-warning are alike for people who will not believe, a direct boundary on prophetic exhortation.
The Quran warns whoever is living, usefully contrasting spiritually responsive life with the focus's dead.
Hearts are covered and ears deaf before the message, with a separating veil, closely explaining blocked reception.
The Quran is deafness in the ears and blindness for rejecters, a direct account of guidance remaining inaccessible.
Following desire ends in a seal on hearing, heart, and sight, giving a causal analogue for the focus.
Granted hearing, sight, and hearts avail nothing when God's signs are denied, distinguishing faculties from response.
Some listen to the messenger but depart unchanged; this supplies a social instance of ineffective hearing.
The question of locked hearts gives a compact image of why the Quran is not pondered.
The condemned admit that listening or reasoning would have prevented their ruin, directly joining hearing and understanding.
Turning away from the reminder presents a vivid later parallel to the focus's withdrawal from the call.
